Let $\pmb{y}_i=(y_{i1},\ldots,y_{iJ})'$ be a column vector of $J$ observations for the $i$th individual.  In cognitive psychology, for example, these observations are performance scores in a battery of tasks.  We model these observations as a multivariate normal:
$$
\pmb{y}_i \sim \mathcal{N}_J(\pmb{\mu}, \pmb{\Sigma}),
$$
where $\pmb\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_J)'$ is a column vector of means and $\pmb{\Sigma}$ is a $J\times J$ covariance matrix.  As usual, the covariance may be expressed as a function of correlation matrix $\pmb{\rho}$:
$$
\pmb{\Sigma} = \mathrm{diag}(\pmb{\sigma})\;\; \pmb{\rho}\;\; \mathrm{diag}(\pmb{\sigma}),
$$
where $\mathrm{diag}(\pmb{\sigma})$ is a diagonal matrix with diagonal elements $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_J$.  

This covariance matrix is the object of interest, and in SEM it is decomposed as
$$
\pmb{\Sigma} =\pmb{\Lambda}\pmb{\Phi}\pmb{\Lambda}^{\prime} + \pmb{\Psi}.
$$
Here $\pmb{\Lambda}$ is the $J \times K$ loading matrix relating $J$ observed tasks to $K$ latent factors. The $K \times K$ factor covariance matrix $\pmb{\Phi}$ encodes covariation among the factors, and $\pmb{\Psi}=\mathrm{diag}(\psi_{1},\ldots,\psi_{J})$ is the $J\times J$ diagonal task-specific residual covariance matrix. The implication of this diagonal formulation is that residuals are mutually uncorrelated across tasks. This decomposition separates $\pmb{\Sigma}$ into a common component, $\pmb{\Lambda}\pmb{\Phi}\pmb{\Lambda}^{\prime}$, that captures shared covariation among tasks and a task-specific component, $\pmb{\Psi}$, that captures the remaining task variance not explained by the common part. Factor models are then specified by placing restrictions on $\pmb{\Lambda}$ (and sometimes on $\pmb{\Phi}$), yielding either confirmatory (restricted) or exploratory (less restricted) formulations.

ICM-CFA is a restricted factor model in which each task loads on one and only one factor. For example, with $J=6$ tasks and $K=2$ factors, if Tasks 1 through 3 are taken to measure one construct and Tasks 4 through 6 another, the loading matrix may be specified as:
$$
\pmb{\Lambda} \;=\;
\begin{bmatrix}
  \lambda_{1} & 0 \\
  \lambda_{2} & 0 \\
  \lambda_{3} & 0 \\
  0 & \lambda_{4} \\
  0 & \lambda_{5} \\
  0 & \lambda_{6}
\end{bmatrix}.
$$
This specification of $\pmb{\Lambda}$ encodes a perfect-cluster structure where tasks load on their assigned factor and off-factor loadings are fixed to zero. Covariation between tasks in different clusters is therefore attributed to association between the two latent factors, encoded in the factor covariance matrix $\pmb{\Phi}$.


There are two equivalent parameterizations commonly used to set the scale of the model. We describe them using the six-task, two-factor example above. Both apply to any number of tasks and factors by imposing the same identifying restriction separately for each factor. The first fixes one loading per factor to 1.0; in the present example, $\lambda_1=\lambda_4=1$. This sets the factor scales while leaving the factor variances free to be estimated. In the second parameterization each factor variance is fixed to 1.0. No loadings are fixed, and the factor covariance matrix is therefore a correlation matrix. For example,
$$
\pmb{\Phi} \;=\;
\begin{bmatrix}
  1 &  \varphi \\
  \varphi & 1
\end{bmatrix},
$$
where $\varphi$ is the correlation between the two factors.  Without loss of generality, we use this second parameterization throughout.

The latent correlation $\varphi$ may be interpreted as the correlation between latent scores. An equivalent formulation, obtained by introducing latent scores and conditioning on them, is
$$
\pmb{y}_i|\pmb{\eta}_i \sim \mathcal{N}_J(\pmb{\mu}+\pmb{\Lambda}\pmb{\eta}_i, \pmb{\Psi}),
$$
where $\pmb{\eta}_i=(\eta_{i1},\ldots,\eta_{iK})'$ is a vector of latent scores for the $i$th individual, distributed as $\pmb{\eta}_i\sim \mathcal{N}_K(\pmb{0},\pmb{\Phi})$. The correlation between scores in the two-factor example is $\mathrm{cor}(\eta_{i1},\eta_{i2}) = \varphi$.
